questions.q: In the lesson's `zero_state(2)` function, what does the returned array represent, and why does only index 0 get set to 1.0?
options: It represents |11>, since index 0 is counted from the highest basis state
Index 0 is set to 1.0 arbitrarily and has no connection to any basis state
It represents a fully mixed state with equal probability everywhere
It represents the 2-qubit basis state |00>, and index 0 corresponds to |00> in the standard basis ordering, matching what np.kron([1,0],[1,0]) would also produce
questions.explain: zero_state builds |00...0> directly as an all-zeros array with a 1 in the first slot, which is exactly what Chapter 2's Kronecker-product construction of |00> also produces -- the capstone just builds it directly rather than via np.kron.

questions.q: The lesson verifies that applying `H (x) I` to the state [1,0,0,0] gives [0.707107, 0, 0.707107, 0]. What does this intermediate state represent?
options: An invalid, unnormalized state vector
(|00> + |10>)/sqrt(2) -- qubit 0 is in superposition while qubit 1 is still definitely 0
The final Bell state, with both qubits already entangled
A state where qubit 1 is in superposition and qubit 0 is fixed at 0
questions.explain: Only positions 0 and 2 (|00> and |10>) are nonzero, meaning qubit 0 (the first/leftmost label) varies while qubit 1 stays 0 -- entanglement between the qubits hasn't happened yet; that's what the following CNOT step produces.

questions.q: After applying CNOT to [0.707107, 0, 0.707107, 0], the lesson shows the result is [0.707107, 0, 0, 0.707107]. Why does the amplitude move from position 2 to position 3, rather than staying at position 2 or moving somewhere else?
options: CNOT always moves every amplitude to the last position in the vector regardless of the input
CNOT randomly redistributes amplitude among all four positions
The amplitude doesn't actually move; the printed output in the lesson contains an error
Position 2 corresponds to |10>, where the control qubit is |1>, so CNOT flips the target qubit from 0 to 1, landing the amplitude at position 3 (|11>); position 0 (|00>, control=0) is left unchanged
questions.explain: CNOT's defining behavior is: flip the target qubit only when the control qubit is 1. Position 2 (|10>) has control=1, so it maps to position 3 (|11>); position 0 (|00>, control=0) stays put -- exactly the Bell-state entanglement pattern.

questions.q: Why does the lesson emphasize verifying each step (the H(x)I step, then the CNOT step) separately rather than just trusting that `apply_gates([kron_gate(H, I), CNOT], zero_state(2))` produces 'the Bell state' because that's the textbook recipe?
options: Because `apply_gates` does not actually work and must be checked by hand every time it is called

Step-by-step verification catches a subtle bug like accidentally writing `kron_gate(I, H)` instead of `kron_gate(H, I)`, which would silently produce a different, still-plausible-looking, but wrong entangled state
Because NumPy's matrix multiplication is known to be unreliable for 4x4 matrices
There is no real benefit; the lesson does this purely as a formatting convention
questions.explain: The danger with recipe-following code is a swapped argument order producing a wrong-but-plausible result; verifying each intermediate step against a hand-computed fact is exactly what catches that kind of silent bug.

questions.q: What is the functional difference between `apply_gate` and `apply_gates` in the capstone's `simulate.py`?
options: They are identical functions with two different names for convenience
`apply_gate` evolves the state by exactly one gate via matrix-vector multiplication; `apply_gates` applies a whole list of gates to the state in sequence, modeling a small circuit
`apply_gate` only works for single-qubit states, while `apply_gates` only works for multi-qubit states
`apply_gates` recomputes the gate matrices from scratch, while `apply_gate` uses precomputed ones
questions.explain: apply_gates is built directly on top of apply_gate -- it just loops over a list of gates, calling apply_gate once per gate, to model a sequence of operations (a small circuit) in order.
